opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few big ones. The first is just reliability over long horizons. A model can be really impressive on a single step, but when you string together dozens or hundreds of actions, small error rates compound, and the agent can go off the rails in ways that are hard to recover from. A good coworker notices when something's gone wrong and course-corrects, and getting models to do that consistently is still hard.

The second is context. When you hire someone, a huge part of what makes them useful over time is that they learn how your team works: what tools you use, what your preferences are, where things live, who to ask. Agents today mostly start fresh each time, so figuring out memory and personalization in a way that actually feels like working with someone who knows you is a big open problem.

Third is knowing when to ask versus when to just go. If an agent checks in on every little thing, it's annoying and you might as well have done it yourself. But if it never asks, it might take actions you didn't want, especially ones that are hard to undo, like sending an email or making a purchase. Calibrating that, and having the model understand which actions are high-stakes, is really important for trust.

And then there's the interface question. Do you want to watch the agent work, or hand something off and come back later? I think a lot of the value comes from being able to delegate tasks asynchronously and trust they'll get done well, but getting to that level of trust requires all the other pieces to work. So it's a mix of model capability, product design, and safety, all at once.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because the gap between a really impressive demo and something you'd actually trust to do work alongside you is enormous. There are a few things that stand out to me.

The first is reliability over long horizons. A coworker doesn't just do one task well; they do a chain of fifty small tasks, and if they get one of them wrong, they notice and recover. With agents, errors compound. If each step is 95 percent reliable, by the time you're twenty steps in, you're in bad shape. So a lot of the work is less about raw capability on a single step and more about the model being able to check its own work, realize it's gone down the wrong path, back up, and try something else. That's really what made Deep Research work, honestly: it wasn't that the model could read a web page, it was that it could read a hundred of them, change its mind, and keep going.

The second is context. A good coworker knows the history of the project, what you tried last week, what the team's conventions are, what you actually meant when you wrote a vague Slack message. Agents today mostly start from zero every time, or they have access to tools but not to the tacit knowledge that makes someone useful. Giving a model the right information at the right time, and letting it ask for clarification when it genuinely needs it rather than guessing, is a surprisingly hard product and research problem.

And then there's the trust piece. A coworker earns autonomy gradually. Nobody hands a new hire the production credentials on day one. So I think a lot of what we have to figure out is the interface: how does the agent show its work, when does it stop and check in, how does the user calibrate how much to delegate. If you ask for permission too often, it's not actually saving anyone time. If you never ask, people won't let it touch anything important. Getting that balance right, and having the model itself be good at judging which situation it's in, is maybe the thing I'm most excited about right now.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is figuring out what context the agent needs to do the job well. When you ask a coworker to do something, there’s a lot you don’t explicitly say. They know what you’re working toward, they know some of your preferences, and they know who to ask if something is unclear. An agent needs a way to get that context without making you explain everything every time.

Then there’s reliability over longer tasks. It needs to do more than take one good action. It needs to keep track of what it’s trying to accomplish, recognize when something didn’t work, and recover. Even small errors can compound when there are lots of steps.

And I think knowing when to involve you is really important. If it asks you about every decision, you end up managing it so closely that it’s not saving you much work. But if it makes assumptions about everything, it can go quite far in the wrong direction. A good coworker makes progress independently and brings you in when your judgment actually matters. Getting that balance right is a big part of making agents useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is that a coworker doesn’t just answer a question. They take an underspecified task, figure out what information they need, do some work, and come back to you when they need input. Getting that whole loop right is much harder than getting a good response to a single prompt.

There’s a context problem: what does the agent need to know about your goals, your team, and the tools you use? And then there’s a reliability problem. If it has to take a lot of steps, small mistakes can compound. It needs to recognize when something went wrong and recover, rather than keep going based on a bad assumption.

I also think knowing when to ask for help is a really important part of this. If it asks you about every little thing, you’re doing the work of managing it. If it never asks, it might spend a long time doing the wrong thing. A useful agent needs to make progress independently while giving you the right opportunities to steer it.
